# Introduction \label{Introduction}
This report does a brief comparison the concentration, risk exposures , volatility, returns and active share between JSE indexes. Specifically the CappedSWIX (which is the benchmark), LargeCaps, MidCaps and SmallCaps. 


# Index 'Composition
The graph belows shows the different sector exposures of the indexes over time:
CappedSWIX: Its largest exposure has been industrials since the beginning of the sample. Since 2017 resources has been occupying an increasing share in the index.
LargeCaps: Resources has been decreasing and financials increasing.
MidCaps:Already much more variation overtime than the above. Resources adn financials are increasing its share where industrials have largely declined.
SmallCaps: Unclassified share has decreased. Has by far the highest exposure to properties of all the Indexes. Share of industrials has been increasing.
```{r sector_growth, out.width = "100%"}
include_graphics(fig_path("sector_exposure"))
```

The Herfindahl-Hirschman Index (HHI) measures portfolio concentration by summing the squared weights of all holdings (\(\sum w_i^2\)), heavily penalizing large, dominant positions. Taking its inverse (1/HHI) reveals the effective number of stocks, showing how many equal-weighted holdings an index truly behaves like. 
```{r}
include_graphics(fig_path("concentration"))
```
- CappedSWIX (red): Rebounded sharply in 2017 from severe concentration lows (~20 effective stocks) to stabilize between 30 and 40. This shift reflects the JSE's introduction of a 10% single-stock capping limit at quarterly rebalances, which curbed the outsized dominance of mega-caps like Naspers by redistributing excess weight across smaller constituents.
- LargeCaps (green): Historically exhibit the highest concentration (hovering between 10 and 17 effective stocks), before experiencing a notable structural improvement in diversification after 2022 to sit above 20.
- MidCaps (teal): Have steadily grown more concentrated over the past decade, declining from highs above 40 effective stocks toward the mid-20s.
- SmallCaps (purple): Consistently remain the most diversified index, fluctuating between 35 and 49 effective stocks, though trending slightly lower in recent years.
\newpage
The table below show the average concentration, effective number of stocks and the weight of the top 5 and 10 stocks in each index.
```{r conc_tab}
read_tab("concentration_summary") %>%
  kable(digits = 2, booktabs = TRUE, caption = "Average concentration by index")
```

# Index Risk Profile
GARCH models offer noise reduced volatility estimates. The GARCH model family has models tremendously and the results of different can be found in the appendix. The graph below shows the volatility from an eGARCH model. Interestingly the results show that SmallCaps have less "structure" in their volatility meaning they are just extra noisy as the most volatility. These stocks often dont trade much so some trades can cause significant price changes.

```{r}
include_graphics(fig_path("eGARCH_vol"))
```
In the graph below the median constituent volatility is plotted for each index on a rolling 60-day basis. As to be expected SmallCaps have higher volatility than the other indexes and LargeCaps having the least.
```{r}
include_graphics(fig_path("constituent_vol"))
```

The results in the table below shows the annualised stnadard deviationa sn returns for periods of high, medium and low volatility. Where the the high-vol regime corresponds to the times where the vol was in the top third of its distribution , low-vol to bottom third and mid-vol to middle.
```{r regime_tab}
read_tab("regime_table") %>%
  kable(digits = 3, booktabs = TRUE, caption = "Performance by volatility regime")
```

# Index Return Profile
Examining rolling annualised returns over 1-year and 3-year horizons illustrates how return dispersion and cyclicality behave across JSE market-capitalisation tiers:
- High Short-Term Cyclicality (1Y): Over 1-year rolling windows, all four indices move largely in sync with broad macroeconomic shocks, dropping into negative territory during the early-2020 market sell-off before rebounding sharply. SmallCaps (purple) exhibit the greatest upside amplitude, surging past 120% during the 2021 recovery, whereas LargeCaps (green) and CappedSWIX (red) track closely together with more moderated peaks.
- Smoothed Long-Term Trajectories (3Y): Extending the horizon to 3-year rolling periods substantially dampens short-term noise, revealing a steady upward return trend from 2020 onward. SmallCaps outperforms on a 3-year rolling basis post-2021 until 2025 peaking near 50% in early 2023—while MidCaps (teal) frequently lag the broader benchmark over extended periods.
```{r}
include_graphics(fig_path("rolling_returns"))
```

```{r risk_tab}
read_tab("risk_return_summary") %>%
  kable(digits = 3, booktabs = TRUE, caption = "Risk and return summary")
```
# Index Active Share
Active share measures the percentage of a portfolio's holdings that differ from the benchmark index, ranging from 0% (an identical replica) to 100% (no overlapping holdings). Because the Capped SWIX is a market-capitalisation-weighted benchmark dominated by large-cap equities, active share increases dramatically as one moves down the size spectrum:
```{r}
include_graphics(fig_path("active_share"))
```

- LargeCaps (Mean: 26.8%): Exhibit the lowest active share (ranging from 12.9% to 33.2%), reflecting substantial constituent overlap with the Capped SWIX. Notably, LargeCap active share dropped sharply after 2023—falling below 20%—indicating an even tighter alignment with the benchmark's top holdings.
- MidCaps (Mean: 79.4%): Offer significant structural differentiation from the benchmark (ranging between 69.3% and 87.3%), though their active share trended gradually downward between 2017 and 2024 before rebounding toward 80% recently.
- SmallCaps (Mean: 95.3%): Maintain a near-total divergence from the Capped SWIX across the entire sample period (ranging from 91.8% to 96.9%), confirming that small-cap equities represent an almost entirely distinct opportunity set from the primary JSE benchmark.


```{r as_tab}
read_tab("active_share_summary") %>%
  kable(digits = 3, booktabs = TRUE, caption = "Active share versus the Capped SWIX")
```
# Conclusion
Comparing these South African Indices we again see that the market compensates risk, as different indexes perfrom better in higher vol regimes, SmallCaps outperforming during low- and mid-vol regimes. Industrials are a major part of SOuth African indices and Financials earning a larger share. Since 2020 SA indices apart from LargeCaps have become less diversified.

```{r ic_tab}
library(kableExtra)

read_tab("ic_tables") %>%
  filter(Criterion %in% c("Akaike", "Bayes")) %>%
  pivot_longer(c(sGARCH, gjrGARCH, eGARCH, apARCH),
               names_to = "Model", values_to = "Value") %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = Model, values_from = Value) %>%
  arrange(Criterion, Index) %>%
  select(-Criterion) %>%
  kable(digits = 3, booktabs = TRUE,
        caption = "Information criteria by model and index") %>%
  pack_rows("Akaike", 1, 4) %>%
  pack_rows("Bayes", 5, 8) %>%
  kable_styling(latex_options = c("hold_position", "scale_down"))


```
